role: Food production safety officer in a meat plant's further-processing workshop
headline: The food production safety officer at a mid-sized meat-processing plant in Luohe, Henan, guarding the metal detectors, retorts and cold chain of the ham sausage and chilled meat workshops, and signing the daily control sheet every day
unit: A large integrated meat company in Luohe running from slaughter to further processing; its processing workshops turn out several hundred tons of ham sausage, cooked smoked sausage and chilled meat products a day
level: You've just passed the food safety officer training and assessment, and can do the daily controls and weekly inspection on your own. You know HACCP, but when it comes to whether to stop a line, you still phone your supervisor first
intro: You worked two years in quality control at this plant, going from testing nitrite with strips to checking a whole workshop's risk control list from start to finish on your own. Luohe is a city that grew up on meat products, and families here have worked at the plant for two generations. As of today, behind the daily control sheet you sign are the hundreds of tons of sausage that go out every day to supermarket shelves across China.
salary_note: Estimate: a quality job at a large Luohe meat plant pays somewhat below the national figure, but comes with a canteen, a dormitory and product perks at year end; in the months of stocking up before Mid-Autumn and Spring Festival there's a bit more overtime.

facts.label: Food Production Safety Officer (current level)
facts.value: 1-3 years, ¥6,120–9,000 a month (national average, estimated from pay by experience)

facts.label: Next level up
facts.value: Food Safety Supervisor / Quality Supervisor (3-6 years)

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Stopping a batch of raw material that arrived above cold-chain temperature

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Doing and recording the day's control checks against the risk control list

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 7 related job listings nationwide, 0 in this city (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: Before the workshop: the disinfectant foot bath, hand washing, the dryer, the air shower, white overalls and rubber boots. At the changing-room door you spot-check a few workers' nails and gloves.

First job is testing the metal detector. You push the test pieces, a ferrous ball and a stainless steel ball, through the machine inside sausages one by one, and each one has to set it off and get kicked off the line before you tick the record.

Receiving raw material. Cut meat comes up from the cold store; you probe the core temperature, three degrees, then go through the post-slaughter inspection certificate and batch number. Only when they match does it go into the batching room.
The filling line clatters along, a row of machines. You stand in the ingredients room watching the weigher measure out nitrite gram by gram, and sign your name on the two-person verification sheet.
The plant canteen: braised noodles with two of the plant's own sausages. The old hand across the table says when he joined, this line was still filled by hand.
With sterile swabs you sample the floor drains, conveyor belts and knives in the chilling room, seal them in tubes, label them and send them to the lab for Listeria.
On the retort, the temperature curve has dropped two degrees for one minute. You quarantine and tag that load, and phone for the equipment and production supervisors to come look.

You enter today's daily control records into the system and sign. Riding your e-bike back to the dormitory along the Sha River, people are square-dancing on the bank, and there's a smell of smoked meat on the evening breeze.

ladder.title: Workshop QC Inspector / Quality Controller
ladder.focus: In-process inspection, hygiene checks and records, learning the regulations and standards.

ladder.title: Food Production Safety Officer
ladder.focus: Pass the training and assessment, run daily controls and weekly inspections, manage records and staff health.

ladder.title: Food Safety Supervisor / Quality Supervisor
ladder.focus: Build the HACCP system, manage supplier audits, handle incidents and cooperate with investigations.

ladder.title: Food Safety Director
ladder.focus: A post special-food and large and medium enterprises are required to have: oversee the system and report monthly to the head of the company.

ladder.title: Head of Quality / Quality Director
ladder.focus: The company's top person responsible for quality and food safety.

ai_tasks.name: Doing and recording the day's control checks against the risk control list
ai_tasks.how: AI can turn the list into a phone form, compile records automatically, flag abnormal items and generate a zero-risk report. A person has to go into the workshop to look, smell and touch, deal with problems found on the spot, and sign for the result.

ai_tasks.name: Organizing this week's hazard inspection and writing the weekly report
ai_tasks.how: AI can summarize a week of daily check data, classify hazards, draft the weekly report from a template and track corrective progress. A person organizes each department's on-site inspection, judges how serious each hazard is, and pushes the fixes through.

ai_tasks.name: Stopping a batch of raw material that arrived above cold-chain temperature
ai_tasks.how: AI can take data from the temperature logger, raise an alarm and generate a record when it's out of range. Rechecking the temperature at receiving, deciding whether to reject or quarantine, and arguing it out face to face with the supplier and driver must be decided and answered for by a person.

ai_tasks.name: Preparing the monthly food safety review meeting materials
ai_tasks.how: AI can pretty much turn daily checks, weekly inspections, corrective ledgers and training records into charts and a draft presentation on its own. A person only needs to check the data definitions, add the issues that need a decision from management, and spot-check it once.

ai_tasks.name: Responding when a failed metal detector puts a batch at risk of foreign bodies
ai_tasks.how: AI can help pull the traceability range quickly from batch records and draft the incident record. Whether to stop the line after a metal detector fails, and which products to quarantine or recall, involve on-site verification and serious responsibility, and must be decided by a person and reported to management.

ai_tasks.name: Writing the HACCP plan for a new product line
ai_tasks.how: AI can draft the hazard analysis table from the recipe and process flow, list possible critical control points and reference limits, and produce training slides. A person checks it against the plant's own equipment and real process, sets the critical limits, gets front-line staff to carry it out, and is responsible for the plan.

events.e_metal: Going through the records, you find the night shift skipped the metal detector test pieces for two hours. Every product from those two hours goes back through the machine, and it pulls out one sausage with a broken needle in it. The workshop director says nothing and signs your report.
events.e_stop_line: You recommend stopping the line to investigate a temperature anomaly, and the production supervisor says it's a rush order for a supermarket, they can't afford to stop. It goes up to the plant manager, the line stops for forty minutes, and the cause is a broken probe; the product is fine. For that month you don't quite dare raise your head in the workshop.
events.e_holiday: Stocking up before Spring Festival, the workshop runs three shifts and there isn't a day off for a month. You sign the daily control sheet three times a day, and there are five alarms set on the clock in your dormitory.
events.e_cold: The chilling and packing rooms are always below ten degrees. In and out dozens of times a day, hot and cold and hot again, you catch one cold after another all winter.
events.e_audit_pass: An audit team from a fast-food chain spends three days at the plant, going through the HACCP plan, checking traceability and running a mock recall. In two hours you trace one batch from the pig farm to thirteen restaurants, and the auditor writes 'excellent' in the report.
events.e_love: A new colleague in the lab always asks one more question when you bring in swabs: which workshop is this from? Later the two of you go to the lantern show at the food festival, crowds pressing in, and neither of you lets go.
events.e_swine_fever: An outbreak of swine fever is reported in another province, and every raw material batch at the plant needs extra testing. For two weeks you run back and forth between the lab and the workshop, and every truckload's test report passes through your hands.
events.e_ai_form: The plant's daily control checks move onto a phone form: the system compiles and flags anomalies automatically, and the daily zero-risk report generates at a tap. You save the time you spent copying sheets, but your supervisor says: no problems on the form doesn't mean no problems in the workshop.
events.e_cert: The company sends you to qualify as a HACCP internal auditor. When you come back you redo the hazard analysis for the chilled meat line and add one more critical control point: the ambient temperature of the slicing room.
events.e_complaint: A consumer posts a video saying they bit into something hard in a sausage. You pull that batch's metal detector records and production footage through the night, and it turns out to be a small piece of cartilage. The PR department replies using the statement you wrote.
events.e_wedding: You hold your wedding in Luohe, and the cold platter at the banquet has the plant's sausages on it. A few colleagues eat and guess which line they came off.
events.e_supplier_fail: On a site audit of a sausage casing supplier you find they wash with well water and have no test reports. You mark them as failing, and the next day the supplier's owner drives to the plant and goes looking for three different people.
events.e_inspection: The provincial market regulator does a surprise inspection, walking straight into the workshop without warning. They pull three batching records and two metal detector records, then ask a worker what the disinfectant concentration is. The worker gets it right, and behind him you let out your breath.
events.e_house: You buy a three-bedroom flat in western Luohe, about ¥200,000 down, half of it from your parents. From the new balcony you can see the plant's chimneys.
events.e_baby: Your daughter is born. Mixing her formula, you glance at the production date and batch number on the tin without thinking.
events.e_ai_trace: The plant brings in a traceability system: scan the code on a pack and in one second you see which farm the pig came from, which day it was slaughtered, which line filled it and who signed off. A mock recall goes from two hours to ten minutes.
events.e_ai_report: For the monthly review meeting with the plant manager, AI can pull the data, make the charts and write the first draft on its own. Your job becomes checking the data definitions and writing in the two problems it didn't see.
events.e_mentor: A quality controller you trained stops a truck of over-temperature raw material on her own for the first time, arguing with the driver by the truck for half an hour. She comes back and tells you: I had a thermometer in my hand, I wasn't afraid of him.
events.e_knee: The workshop floor is wet and slippery, and you fall at the door of the chilling room; your knee is swollen for two weeks. After that, your rubber boots are the non-slip kind.
events.e_parent: Your father goes into hospital back home in Zhoukou, and you take a week off. When the ward meal arrives, the first thing you check is whether it's hot or cold.
events.e_system: The food safety management system you led the revision of is rolled out by the group to six plants in other provinces. When a new plant starts up, the first binder sent to its quality department is that one.
events.e_young: There are fewer and fewer young workers; half the filling line is old hands over fifty. The plant starts installing automated packing lines, and one line goes from thirty people to eight.

c_stop.title: Stop this line or not
c_stop.situation: At three in the afternoon, one pass of a metal detector test piece fails to be rejected; a little later it's normal again. By the rules, everything since the machine's last passed test has to be quarantined and rechecked: over an hour and several tons of sausage. The production supervisor says maybe the test piece was placed off-center.

options.label: Stop the line, quarantine and recheck
options.result: You hang the stop-line sign and call the equipment department. Several tons of product go through the machine again and nothing is found; the cause is the probe's sensitivity drifting. That evening the supervisor buys you a bowl of hot pepper soup and says nothing else.

options.label: Test three more times first
options.result: You test three more times, and all three are normal. You write down that one failure and the three results after it, and have the equipment department calibrate it the next day.

c_haccp.title: Lead the HACCP plan for a new product line, aiming for Food Safety Supervisor
c_haccp.situation: The plant is starting a ready-meal line, frozen braised pork and preserved-vegetable pork packs, and needs someone to write the HACCP plan from scratch: hazard analysis, critical control points, critical limits. Do it well and you're first in line for Food Safety Supervisor next year, but for those six months you'd be running between two places.

options.label: Take it on
options.result: You spend six months on the trial line, measuring the temperature and time of every step. The day you hand in the plan, your supervisor puts a tick beside the critical limits on page three.

options.label: Hold the old workshop first
options.result: You say the old workshop isn't sorted out yet, and you don't want to split your attention. Someone else writes the plan, two problems come up in the trial run, and they both come to you.

c_zhengzhou.title: Move to a frozen food plant in Zhengzhou
c_zhengzhou.situation: A university classmate is quality supervisor at a big frozen food plant in Zhengzhou and says they need a safety officer who knows meat products: thirty percent more pay, but you'd rent in Zhengzhou and only get back to Luohe on weekends.

options.label: Go to Zhengzhou
options.result: New plant, new products, from sausages to glutinous rice balls and dumplings. You find the things you manage are different, but the line you hold is the same.

options.label: Stay in Luohe
options.result: You say Luohe is close to home and housing is cheap. Your classmate says then I'll keep asking you when things come up, and you say fine.

c_ai_flow.title: Design the human-machine on-site inspection process
c_ai_flow.situation: The company wants to bring cameras, temperature probes and metal detector data into one system with AI raising alerts automatically, and needs a safety officer to set the rules: which alerts need someone on site, which can be checked remotely. Some say one person will soon be able to cover three workshops.

options.label: Lead the rules
options.result: You turn every anomaly you've seen over the years into a rule, and spell out which things only someone standing in the workshop can see. After it goes live, the times you're called out at night drop by half.

options.label: Look after your own workshop
options.result: You say what happens on site still has to be seen on site. Someone else sets the rules; there are two you think are wrong, and you raise them at a meeting.

c_supervisor.title: Compete for Food Safety Supervisor / Quality Supervisor
c_supervisor.situation: The quality department is naming a Food Safety Supervisor to run the HACCP system, supplier audits and incident response for the whole processing site. To compete you present a risk event you handled and defend it in front of several workshop directors, whose workshops you'd be inspecting from then on.

options.label: Put your name in
options.result: You talk about those two hours when the metal detector went untested, from going through the records to pulling out the broken needle. One workshop director in the room says, that was my workshop.

options.label: Leave it to an older colleague
options.result: You think old Liu, with twenty years at the plant, can stand up to the workshop directors better than you, and don't apply. Once he's in the job, he gives you the hardest workshops to inspect.

c_auditor.title: Become a food safety auditor at a certification body
c_auditor.situation: A certification body in Zhengzhou is hiring food system auditors with company experience and an internal auditor certificate. You'd travel by project, auditing systems in other people's plants, no longer tied to one workshop, for about the same pay.

options.label: Become an auditor
options.result: Checklist in hand, you walk into an unfamiliar plant for the first time, and the first thing you go to look at is still their metal detector test records.
options.end: You became a food safety auditor, visiting forty or fifty plants a year, from infant formula to spicy gluten snacks. In a pile of perfectly neat records, you can always find the one page where the ink is too fresh.

options.label: Stay at the plant
options.result: You say you still like watching over your own workshop every day. The man from the certification body leaves a card, and you tuck it into your HACCP certificate.

c_director.title: Become the plant's Food Safety Director
c_director.situation: By regulation the plant must have a food safety director who reports risks to the plant manager every month and is the first held accountable if something major happens. The plant manager asks if you'll take it: your signature will weigh differently, and you'll spend less and less time in the workshops.

options.label: Take the director post
options.result: Every month you sit across from the plant manager and go through the risks page by page. Once you recommend dropping a major supplier; he frowns at it a long while, and nods.

options.label: Stay as supervisor
options.result: You say you want a few more years in the workshops. The group sends a director, who often calls on you in meetings to ask what's really happening on the floor.

c_consult.title: Go into food safety consulting
c_consult.situation: A former customer auditor has started his own consultancy, helping small and medium food plants build food safety systems and prepare for inspections, and wants you as a partner. Income depends on projects: in good times double what you earn now, with no projects, nothing.

options.label: Go into consulting
options.result: You quit and drive all over Henan to small food plants.
options.end: You became a food safety consultant, teaching one workshop-sized factory after another to write risk lists, test metal detectors and keep samples. Some owners found you fussy at first; later, every holiday, they send you a box of their own products.

options.label: Stay at the plant
options.result: You say a big plant is steadier. He says then when a difficult factory comes along, I'll ask you to come take a look, and you say fine.

c_quality_head.title: Become the group's Quality Director
c_quality_head.situation: The group wants one person to run the quality and food safety system across a dozen-odd plants nationwide, dealing with regulators, major customers and the press. It means half the year away, and whatever happens, you're the first one who has to stand up and speak.

options.label: Take it on
options.result: You fly across most of China, and at every new plant's kickoff you say the same thing: test the metal detector every two hours, and never miss once.

options.label: Hand it to someone younger
options.result: You recommend a supervisor you trained. The first call she makes after taking over is to ask how to read the retort curves at a plant in another province.

endings.retire: On your last day you walk once round the processing workshop. The metal detector test pieces are automatic now, pushing themselves through every two hours, a row of green lights on the screen. You stand by the filling line watching the sausages come out link by link, and remember the smell of smoked meat on your first day in the workshop, exactly the same as now.
endings.burnout: That winter, after three months of night shifts in stocking-up season, your knees and your sleep give out, and several numbers on your checkup are in red. The plant moves you to the quality department to handle records and training, regular hours. When you teach new hires, the first slide is still the metal detector test record sheet.

stages: You guard the processing workshop's risk control list on your own. Every day you check from the changing room through the ingredients room, filling line, retorts and chilling room, testing metal detectors, checking temperatures and the batching verification sheets, stopping things on the spot when they're wrong and writing it up on the spot; once a week you take the workshop director through the weekly inspection and chase the fixes to the end. The workshop director is twenty years older than you, and you have to learn to say no politely.

You run the food safety system for the whole processing site. Every week you chair the quality meeting, review each workshop's daily controls and weekly inspections, and revise the HACCP plans; every month you audit suppliers on site, and when there's a consumer complaint, a customer audit or a regulatory inspection, you're the one standing in front. When you sign a corrective notice, the workshop director has to reply.

You are the plant's food safety director, reporting to the plant manager at the monthly review and first in line to be held accountable. On your desk are the risk control list, the supplier roster and the recall plan; what you approve is whether to stop a line or change a supplier. When regulators summon the company, you're the one across the table. You rarely test a metal detector now; what you hold is report after signed report.

What you set now is how a dozen-odd plants across the group manage food safety: the system documents, training and assessment, internal audits, recall drills. Half your week is on the road, speaking at new plant kickoffs, answering at major customers' audits, arguing for a testing budget at the group's quality committee. When you do go down to a workshop, you still look at the metal detector test records first.
work: An old hand on the filling line changes casings without changing gloves. You see it on the camera feed and go down to have a word. He mutters that he's been doing this thirty years, and goes to wash his hands and put on a new pair anyway.

A truck of chilled pork arrives, and the trailer's temperature logger shows a stretch at nine degrees. You probe ten spots, three over the limit, and write rejected on the receiving note; the driver spends half an hour on the phone by the truck.
The lab calls: a swab from a chilling room floor drain is positive. You and the cleaning team lead take apart every drain in that area and scrub them, and three days later the resample is negative.
Auditing a spice supplier, you find two unlabeled bags of chili powder in their warehouse. The owner says they're for his own use, and you write in the audit report: fail, correct within a deadline.

A supermarket's quality manager brings you a swollen pack of chilled ham. You pull that batch's retort records and cold-chain temperatures and find the store's display fridge broke down overnight, and write him an explanation.

The new workshop is getting an automated packing line, and the equipment supplier says the metal detector can go after the sealer. You pull out the HACCP plan and insist they move it before boxing, at an extra ¥20,000.
The plant manager wants to switch to a casing supplier twenty percent cheaper. You print that supplier's test records for the past two years and put them on his desk, with a red circle on page two.
You run a plant-wide recall drill, from the customer complaint to retrieving the last box of product: three hours ten minutes. At the review you say next time you want it under two hours.

The market regulator summons the company because one batch's label left out an allergen. You go with the corrective report and set out the cause, the fix and how it will be checked from now on, point by point.

The group has built a new plant in the southwest, and you take two people for the pre-production review. You stand in front of the retorts all afternoon and require the temperature probes to go from one to three.

An overseas customer comes to discuss an export order and asks how you keep standards the same across a dozen plants. You put the group's internal audit data on the screen and walk them through it plant by plant.

The AI system ranks risk across all the group's plants, and last place is a small plant in the north. You don't send a corrective notice straight away; you take the train there first and spend three days in its workshops.
past: You go to middle school in the countryside outside Zhoukou, where half the village's young people work in Luohe's food plants. Your cousin fills sausages at one of them, and when she comes home at New Year with a box of ham sausages, every child in the village comes to share.
In the gaokao (college entrance exam) you get into food quality and safety at a university in Zhengzhou. Your father says with that, you'll know where everything you eat comes from.
In microbiology lab you see, for the first time, the colonies grown from a swab of a chopping board. That evening, in the canteen line, you stare at the cook behind the window a long time.

In the summer of your third year you intern at this Luohe plant, testing nitrite and moisture in the lab, dozens of samples a day. The old lab technician says your hands are steady, you're suited to this.

After graduation you join the plant as a workshop quality controller, sampling, checking temperatures and filling forms on the filling line every day, and studying the Food Safety Law back in the dormitory at night.

Under new regulations the plant puts a full-time food safety officer in every workshop. You take the training and assessment and pass. Your supervisor hands you the risk control list and says: from now on, half of what happens in this workshop is your call.

late.pension_note: Estimate: thirty-odd years of contributions to Luohe's basic pension for company employees on a big plant's wage base, plus a small company annuity, comes to about half your final monthly pay.
scenes: For the first few months of retirement you still glance at your watch every two hours without meaning to. There's no metal detector to test at home, so you go water the plants on the balcony.
The neighborhood asks you to be an adviser to its senior canteen, twice a week, to look over the kitchen. Your first written suggestion: keep the raw and cooked chopping boards apart.
Your daughter graduates from university and joins a testing company. She says everyone in her lab knows Luohe, and you say that's because of the sausages.
In the supermarket you see your old plant's sausages, turn one over to check the production date and batch number, and put it back on the shelf, neatly lined up.
In the quality department you work nine to five, no more night shifts. The first morning you take your child to school, you stand at the gate a long time.

A young safety officer from the workshop calls: a line's retort curve is wrong, and the production supervisor won't let her stop it. You hear her out and say only: quarantine first, then report it, and I'll go with you to talk to him.
When the time comes you retire. Clearing your desk, you find the daily control sheets you filled in by hand in your first year, the writing crooked, a tick after every item.
In the first year away from that workshop, whenever you smell smoked meat, you think of the wet, slippery floor at the chilling room door.

You find your footing in the new place. On trips back to Luohe your old colleagues walk you round the workshop and say the metal detectors test and report on their own now. You say someone still has to watch them.
A quality controller you trained becomes a food safety supervisor and sends you a photo: her teaching new hires about metal detector test pieces, in exactly the words you used.
Later the workshops fill with probes and cameras, and the phone rings at any anomaly. But whether a line stops, someone still has to stand there and make the call.

Your granddaughter asks if you used to make sausages. You say no, you watched other people make them. She asks if that meant you could eat them every day, and you say you ate so many you don't want a single one now.

closing.retire: One evening many years later, walking along the Sha River, a smell of smoked meat drifts over from the plant on the far bank. You stop and breathe it in a while, find nothing wrong, and walk slowly home.
closing.burnout: Many years later you find a metal detector test piece in a drawer, the ferrous ball, though you don't know when you brought it home. You wipe it off and put it back in the drawer.
closing.end: Many years later, in a supermarket in another city, you see a row of sausages made in Luohe, pick one up and look at the batch number. You can't tell which line it came off anymore, and put it back.
